lesson.title: Seeing Ohm's Law in Two Dimensions: The Impedance Triangle
lesson.summary: The impedance triangle is a right triangle with resistance and reactance as legs and impedance magnitude as the hypotenuse, giving a visual, geometric way to find impedance magnitude and the voltage-current phase angle.
lesson.body:
The two numbers that build an impedance, resistance R and reactance X, are literally the two legs of a right triangle, and impedance magnitude is its hypotenuse. Plot R along a horizontal axis and X along a vertical axis, and the line from the origin out to the point (R, X) has length |Z| = sqrt(R^2 + X^2), a direct application of the Pythagorean theorem to the impedance you already met. The angle that line makes with the horizontal R axis is theta = arctan(X/R), and that is not just a geometric curiosity, it is precisely the phase angle by which current lags or leads voltage across that impedance.

The sign of the net reactance decides which way the triangle points and what the phase shift means physically. If inductive reactance dominates, XL greater than XC in a series circuit, or simply X is positive, the triangle tilts upward and theta is positive, meaning current lags voltage, the classic behavior of a motor or transformer winding. If capacitive reactance dominates, X is negative, the triangle tilts downward, and theta is negative, meaning current leads voltage. When a circuit mixes an inductor and a capacitor in series, it is the net reactance, X = XL - XC, that goes into the triangle, since the two reactances work against each other.

Consider a series circuit with resistance R = 8 ohms, inductive reactance XL = 15 ohms, and capacitive reactance XC = 9 ohms. The net reactance is X = 15 - 9 = 6 ohms, giving an impedance Z = 8 + j6 ohms. The triangle's hypotenuse has length |Z| = sqrt(8^2 + 6^2) = sqrt(64 + 36) = sqrt(100) = 10 ohms, and its angle is theta = arctan(6/8) = arctan(0.75) = 36.87 degrees. Since the net reactance is inductive, current lags the source voltage by 36.87 degrees, and a source needs to supply 10 ohms worth of opposition, not simply 8 or 14, to push current through this branch.

The same triangle reappears, scaled up, if you switch from ohms to volts. Suppose 5 A RMS flows through that series branch. The voltage across the resistor is VR = IR = 5 times 8 = 40 V, the net reactive voltage is VX = IX = 5 times 6 = 30 V, and the total source voltage is VZ = IZ = 5 times 10 = 50 V. Check it with the Pythagorean theorem: sqrt(40^2 + 30^2) = sqrt(1600 + 900) = sqrt(2500) = 50, which matches exactly, and the angle between VR and VZ is again arctan(30/40) = 36.87 degrees. The impedance triangle and the voltage triangle are similar triangles, related by the single scale factor of current, which is a handy shortcut once you already know the current in a series branch.

This same geometric pattern, two legs and a hypotenuse tied together by the Pythagorean theorem, is going to reappear later in a different set of units entirely. Once real power, reactive power, and apparent power are defined, they form a power triangle with exactly this shape, because power quantities are simply the voltage and current triangles multiplied together. Getting comfortable reading angles, legs, and hypotenuses off the impedance triangle now pays off directly once the same picture is redrawn in watts and volt-amperes reactive.
